\(\mathrm{D}(f\circ g^n) = \mathrm{D}(f)\,\mathrm{D}(g)\) relation Settled #

Upper bounds — holds for every relation

  • \(\mathrm{D}(f\circ g^n) \le \mathrm{D}(f)\,\mathrm{D}(g)\)
    The obvious algorithm: run an optimal tree for $f$ and answer each of its queries by running an optimal tree for $g$.

Lower bounds / separations — there is a family achieving this

  • \(\mathrm{D}(f\circ g^n) \ge \mathrm{D}(f)\,\mathrm{D}(g)\)
    Savicky02 Tal13 Montanaro14
    Three independent proofs: [Savicky02] (as a lemma towards $\mathrm{D}$ vs $\mathrm{UC}$), [Tal13], and [Montanaro14]. Unlike the randomized case there is no log factor and no counterexample -- deterministic query complexity composes on the nose.
  • \(\mathrm{D}\big(g\circ(f^1,\dots,f^n)\big) = \mathrm{D}\big(\bar g,[\mathrm{D}(f^1),\dots,\mathrm{D}(f^n)]\big)\)
    Montanaro14
    Theorem 2 of [Montanaro14], the general form, and the strongest statement the zoo records here. The outer object $g \subseteq \{0,1\}^n\times Z$ may be a relation; the inner objects $f^i \subseteq X^{m_i}\times\{0,1\}$ may be relations too, but must be Boolean-valued and non-trivial. On the right, $\mathrm{D}(\bar g,[w_1,\dots,w_n])$ is weighted decision tree complexity -- the cheapest tree for $g$ when querying $y_i$ costs $w_i$ -- and $\bar g$ is $g$ with the constant inner objects substituted in. Corollary 3 ($f^1=\dots=f^n$) is the displayed headline, Corollary 4 gives $\mathrm{D}(f^{(k)}) = \mathrm{D}(f)^k$ for the $k$-fold iteration, and Corollary 5 is the deterministic direct sum -- see the dirsum-D record.

The inner alphabet has to be Boolean. Figure 1 of [Montanaro14] exhibits $f:\{0,1\}^2\to\{0,1,2\}$ and $g:\{0,1,2\}^2\to\{0,1,2\}$ with $\mathrm{D}(f)=\mathrm{D}(g)=2$ but $\mathrm{D}(g\circ(f,f)) = 3 < 4$. The reason is the one that makes composition theorems hard in general: the worst-case input for $f$ need not produce a worst-case input for $g$, and with three possible inner answers the outer tree has room to exploit that. An even cheaper illustration with a non-Boolean inner range: take $f = \mathrm{id}:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}^n$ and $g(y)=y_1$, so $\mathrm{D}(f)=n$, $\mathrm{D}(g)=1$, and $\mathrm{D}(g\circ f) = 1$.

Iterating gives cheap amplification of separations, which is what these corollaries are mostly used for: applied to $\mathrm{NAE}_3$ it reproves the Nisan-Szegedy $\mathrm{D}$ vs $\deg$ separation directly, without going through sensitivity.

Contrast with comp-R: for randomized complexity the same statement is false for partial functions and false for relations, and open for total functions.

see also: \(\mathrm{D}(f)\), \(\mathrm{D}^{\mathrm{na}}(f)\), dirsum-D, comp-R, comp-deg, Composition, Direct sum and direct product, \(\mathrm{UC}(f)\) data/relations/04-composition.yaml

\(\mathrm{D}(f^{\otimes k}) = k\,\mathrm{D}(f)\) relation Settled #

Upper bounds — holds for every relation

  • \(\mathrm{D}(f^{\otimes k}) \le k\,\mathrm{D}(f)\)
    Solve the copies one after another.

Lower bounds / separations — there is a family achieving this

  • \(\mathrm{D}(f^{\otimes k}) \ge k\,\mathrm{D}(f),\quad\text{and more generally } \mathrm{D}(f^1,\dots,f^k) = \sum_i \mathrm{D}(f^i)\)
    JainKlauckSantha10 Montanaro14
    Theorem 1 and Corollary 1 of [JainKlauckSantha10], for every relation $f$ and with no loss at all -- one of the few statements in this zoo that is an exact identity. The proof turns a $k$-output tree $T$ into $k$ single-output trees $T_i(v)$ by recursion on the vertices of $T$, and shows $\mathrm{depth}(T) \ge \sum_i \mathrm{depth}(T_i)$. Corollary 5 of [Montanaro14] is the same statement for Boolean-valued relations, as the $g = \mathrm{id}$ case of the composition theorem; [JainKlauckSantha10] allow an arbitrary output alphabet.

Earlier work dismissed this as obvious ("an easy exercise" [NRS94]; "quite uninteresting" because queries do not span instances), and [JainKlauckSantha10] point out that it is not: a single tree that must produce all $k$ outputs is not obviously decomposable into $k$ trees, and in the distributional setting the analogous tight statement is simply false ([Shaltiel04], see dirprod-R). What [NRS94] actually proved is a direct product theorem in the weaker "decision forest" model, where $k$ separate algorithms each produce one output.

The nondeterministic version is genuinely easy: certificate complexity is additive over independent instances.

see also: \(\mathrm{D}(f)\), comp-D, dirsum-R, dirprod-R, Direct sum and direct product, \(\mathrm{C}(f)\) data/relations/04-composition.yaml

    Promise $|x| = n/4$ with $\mathrm{supp}(x)$ inside the odd coordinates or inside the even ones, and ask which. Every input carries $n/4$ ones and each of them names the answer on its own, so probing at random finds a certain answer after four expected queries; an adversary answering $0$ makes a deterministic algorithm exhaust a whole parity class.

The total-function bound $\mathrm{D} = O(\mathrm{R}_0^2)$ goes through $\mathrm{C} \le \mathrm{R}_0$ and $\mathrm{D} \le \mathrm{C}^0\mathrm{C}^1$, and it is the second step that dies here: a promise can leave every certificate one bit long and still hide it, so knowing that a zero-error algorithm stops quickly says nothing about how a deterministic one should search. The first step survives -- $\mathrm{C} \le \mathrm{R}_0$ needs no totality -- and \(\mathrm{Find1}^{\mathrm{par}}_{n}\) has $\mathrm{C} = \mathrm{R}_0 = \Theta(1)$ with $\mathrm{D} = n/4+1$, so it breaks $\mathrm{D}$ vs $\mathrm{C}$ in the same breath.

\(\mathrm{Find1}_{\ge n/2}\) is the same construction as a relation, and the parity label is exactly what is needed to say it about a partial function. Contrast \(\mathrm{GapMaj}^{\delta}_{n}\), the usual partial-setting counterexample, which is no use here: its $\mathrm{R}_0 = \Theta(n)$ matches its $\mathrm{D}$, because the gapped promise leaves no short certificate to find.

  • \(\mathrm{D}(f) \;\ge\; \frac{\mathrm{Var}(f)}{\mathrm{MaxInf}(f)}\)
    OSSS05
    OSSS inequality: $\mathrm{Var}(f) \le \sum_i \delta_i(T)\,\mathrm{Inf}_i(f)$ for every decision tree $T$, where $\delta_i(T)$ is the probability that $T$ queries $i$. Summing, $\sum_i\delta_i(T) \le \mathrm{D}(f)$, so some coordinate has influence at least $\mathrm{Var}(f)/\mathrm{D}(f)$.

OSSS is the standard route from "shallow decision tree" to "influential variable", and is the classical shadow of the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, which asks for the same conclusion from bounded low-degree polynomial instead of shallow decision tree.

see also: \(\mathrm{D}(f)\), \(\mathrm{MaxInf}(f)\), \(\mathrm{I}(f)\), \(\mathrm{I}^{1}(f)\), [AaronsonAmbainis14], The Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture data/relations/05-fourier.yaml
